subject: Pathology
summary: Microsatellite instability (MSI) is a DNA mismatch repair defect that causes rapid mutation of short repeat sequences, driving colorectal and other cancers. It is diagnosed by PCR or IHC and guides therapy and surveillance.

sections.p: MSI is a hypermutator phenotype caused by loss of mismatch repair (MMR) genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2). It is detected by PCR amplification of microsatellite loci or by immunohistochemistry for MMR proteins.
b: IHC for MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2

t.b: Is the tumor MSI‑high, MSI‑low or microsatellite stable? MSI‑high indicates MMR deficiency and suggests Lynch syndrome or sporadic MLH1 hypermethylation.
Loss of a specific protein suggests which gene is mutated; retained proteins rule out that gene.

sections.p: MSI status is not staged but classified as MSI‑high, MSI‑low, or MSS. MSI‑high tumors have a better prognosis in colorectal cancer and respond differently to immunotherapy.
The primary cause is germline mutation of MMR genes (Lynch syndrome). Sporadic MSI arises from MLH1 promoter hypermethylation, often in older patients.

Patients often present with colorectal cancer at a younger age, right‑sided tumors, and a family history of Lynch‑associated cancers. Extracolonic cancers (endometrium, ovary, stomach) may also occur.
b: Family history of colorectal, endometrial, ovarian, gastric cancers

sections.p: Confirm MSI status, screen for germline mutations, and assess for other Lynch‑associated tumors.

t.b: Determines MSI status; MSI‑high suggests Lynch or sporadic MLH1 hypermethylation.
Identifies which MMR protein is lost; guides germline testing.
Presence excludes Lynch syndrome in MSI‑high tumors, indicating sporadic MLH1 hypermethylation.
Identifies patterns suggestive of Lynch syndrome.
Guides surveillance intervals; earlier and more frequent colonoscopies are needed for MSI‑high patients.

sections.p: MSI‑high tumors may be aggressive but respond well to immunotherapy. Untreated Lynch syndrome leads to multiple primary cancers.
Treat the primary tumor per standard oncologic protocols. MSI‑high colorectal cancers benefit from immune checkpoint inhibitors. Surveillance for secondary cancers is essential.
b: PD‑1 inhibitor therapy for MSI‑high metastatic disease

t.b: Is the patient eligible for immunotherapy? MSI‑high status predicts response.
Is adjuvant chemotherapy indicated? MSI‑high patients may have less benefit from 5‑FU alone.

sections.p: Regular colonoscopy every 1–2 years, endometrial surveillance for women, and consideration of prophylactic surgery in high‑risk families.
b: Risk‑reducing hysterectomy and oophorectomy in selected patients

sections.p: MSI is distinct from chromosomal instability (CIN) seen in sporadic colorectal cancers and from polyposis syndromes like FAP.
A normal MSI test does not exclude a germline mutation if the tumor is MSS. BRAF mutation can be absent in sporadic MSI‑high tumors, leading to misclassification.
b: MSS tumor with germline MMR mutation
BRAF V600E negative but MLH1 hypermethylated

whenToSeekHelp: Family history of early‑onset colorectal or endometrial cancer

faq.q: What is the difference between MSI‑high and MSI‑low?
faq.a: MSI‑high shows many unstable microsatellites and indicates MMR deficiency; MSI‑low shows few changes and is usually not clinically significant.

faq.q: Can MSI be found in cancers other than colorectal?
faq.a: Yes, MSI occurs in endometrial, gastric, ovarian, and other cancers, often linked to Lynch syndrome.
Yes, MSI‑high colorectal cancers respond better to PD‑1 inhibitors and may need less aggressive chemotherapy.

exam: Explain how loss of MLH1 leads to microsatellite instability and why this increases cancer risk.
Describe the diagnostic algorithm for a patient with suspected Lynch syndrome, including MSI testing and germline mutation analysis.
Discuss why MSI‑high colorectal cancers respond to PD‑1 inhibitors and how this influences adjuvant therapy decisions.
